title.narrative: Integrated Cholera Response through Case Management and Community-Led Action among conflict affected people in Tawila, North Darfur

description.narrative: ltpgtltbrgtThe April 2025 attacks on Zamzam IDP camp displaced nearly 500,000 people, with over 327,000 arriving in Tawila locality. This unprecedented influx has overwhelmed fragile public services, intensified WASH gaps, and contributed to a rapidly escalating cholera outbreak. As of July 2025, more than 260 cases have been hospitalized, with treatment centers exceeding 100% occupancy. Tawila Umda and Daba Nyara camps—together hosting over 260,000 people—are cholera hotspots. WASH coverage remains critically low, with only 43% accessing safe water and 41% with emergency latrine access. Without urgent intervention, up to 19,000 cholera cases are projected, posing a severe mortality risk, particularly during the rainy season.ltbrgtIn alignment with the SHF Standard Allocation for Tawila/El Fasher, ALIMA proposes an integrated health response to rapidly reduce cholera-related morbidity and mortality among conflict-affected populations. The intervention will focus on:ltbrgtCase Management: Scaling up the Tawila Umda Cholera Treatment Unit (CTU) from 20 to 30 beds and establishing a new 100-bed Cholera Treatment Centre (CTC) in ShokoShoko at the request of the MoH, Cholera Taskforce, and MSF. Facilities will be equipped, staffed, and supplied to manage severe and moderate cases, supported by strengthened triage and isolation protocols.ltbrgtCommunity-Based Care and Surveillance: Establishing and reinforcing Oral Rehydration Points (ORPs) in underserved sites, linked to referral pathways to CTUs/CTCs training community health workers in early case detection, referral, and Infection Prevention and Control (IPC).ltbrgtRisk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE): Delivering targeted cholera prevention messages, mobilizing communities to adopt safe water, sanitation, and hygiene practices, and integrating feedback mechanisms to adapt interventions.ltbrgtThe project will directly target 24,000 people (5927 women, 6169 girls, 4657 men, and 4847 boys), including newly displaced persons, vulnerable host community members, and high-risk groups such as children under five and pregnant/lactating women. An estimated 1400,000 people will benefit indirectly through improved outbreak control measures across Tawila locality.ltbrgtImplementation will be in close coordination with partners under the joint concept note. ALIMA will complement the health interventions of Save the Children International (SCI) and Relief International (RI) and work alongside WASH partners—Solidarités International (SI), Triangle Génération Humanitaire (TGH), and IRC—whose activities will ensure safe water provision, latrine construction, and hygiene promotion in the same locations. Protection partners led by SCI and INTERSOS will address GBV, child protection, and psychosocial needs, ensuring a holistic response.ltbrgtThe integrated approach will maximize impact, avoid duplication, and ensure alignment with cluster technical guidance. Strong linkages with CERF-funded UN agency supply pipelines (UNICEF, WHO, IOM) will secure essential health commodities, while SHF resources will enable ALIMA’s operational delivery. Continuous coordination through Health, WASH, and Protection Clusters and the Tawila Cholera Taskforce will ensure harmonized implementation, geographic complementarity, and efficient use of resources.ltbrgtBy strengthening cholera treatment capacity, enhancing early detection and referral, and promoting community-led prevention, this project will help contain the outbreak before the rainy season ends, save lives, and build community resilience against future WASH-related disease outbreaks in one of Sudan’s most underserved and crisis-affected localitieslt/pgt
